intent: Kept nothing from a previous design, since this is the first proposal. The geometry is a symmetric, central baseline: five 12 mm sensors on a 12 mm pitch spanning 48 mm, placed 40 mm ahead of the axle, so the line is always covered and the look-ahead is short but real. I expect this to complete the oval and s-bend tracks with low rms error. I am considering, without committing yet, a narrower sensor span (for example 0.016 m pitch) if the Integrator finds the signal saturates on tight bends, and a longer look-ahead (y near 0.06) if oscillation is high at speed.
learning: First iteration: no prior race data. The key question for the next proposal is whether the sensor span and look-ahead are the limiting factors, or whether the controller alone governs performance. Integrator feedback on signal range, line-loss frequency and oscillation on each track should decide which geometry parameter to change next.
rationale: Iteration 0 has no race data or Integrator feedback yet, so this proposal rests on the contract's physics and sensing rules rather than evidence. The tape is 25 mm wide, so five sensors spaced 12 mm apart (x = -0.024 to +0.024) with 12 mm footprints always have at least one sensor over the tape near centre, and the outer sensors can see a line that drifts toward the edge. Placing the row 40 mm ahead of the axle gives the Integrator a look-ahead of the line before the wheels reach it, which should reduce the lag that causes oscillation at bends. A 0.12 m wheel track and 0.03 m wheel radius give moderate turning authority without excessive yaw inertia. Body width 0.12 m keeps the off-track limit at 0.0625 m, a little above the 0.06 m floor. A mass of 0.8 kg is mid-range, which keeps acceleration reasonable on the 1.5 m/s average speed the course needs. Expected result: a stable, completing baseline with few line-loss events. This is a deliberately central design to establish a reference point; I will vary sensor span, look-ahead and track width once the Integrator reports how this geometry behaves.
